One take, as an $\mathbb{R}^{88}$-valued step function

804 strikes, 227 seconds, zero dropped packets — the first capture in this project whose timing means anything. What the indicator-function model actually says about how you played, and where the model and the hardware each run out.

1The object

The representation is the one you specified: a note is a scaled indicator on a closed interval, a key is a finite sum of them on pairwise disjoint intervals, and the performance is the direct sum over the 88 keys.

$$f \;=\; \bigoplus_{k=0}^{87} f_k, \qquad f_k \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n_k} P_i\,\mathbf{1}_{[a_i,\,b_i]}, \qquad \lambda\!\left(I_i \cap I_j\right) = 0 \ \ (i \neq j).$$

This take realises it with $n = \sum_k n_k = 804$ strikes distributed over 59 nonzero summands. The disjointness invariant was checked at construction on all 88 tracks and held: no key was reported down twice, and the parser needed no repairs at all — 2240 messages, 804 strikes, 632 pedal events. Every quantity below is a functional of that one object.

the norm ratio is a measurement of the transport, not of the music

$V_{\ell^1}/V_{\ell^\infty} = 1.0187$ on the actuator representation. That ratio is $1$ exactly when no two keys ever change state at the same instant, and it grows with coincidence. Of the 1569 atoms of $Df$, only 32 involve more than one key. Notes overlap constantly — up to 7 keys are down together — but their onsets almost never coincide, and §5 says why: the link puts nearly every packet on its own 5 ms slot, so a chord struck as one gesture is delivered as a 5 ms arpeggio unless the piano happened to bundle it into one packet (53 packets did). This ratio is measuring the transport. On the sounding representation, where a single CC64 message lifts many strings at literally one instant, it rises to 1.452.

2Is $F$ a devil's staircase? No, and here is the distance

The Cantor function is monotone, continuous, and flat off a set of measure zero. $F$ here is monotone, continuous, and flat off a set of measure 17.06 s out of 227.44 s. That is the wrong sign: the exceptional set is not small, it is almost everything.

The sharp statement is about regularity rather than about measure. $F$ is the integral of a bounded function, so it is Lipschitz:

$$|F(t)-F(s)| \;\le\; \Big(\sup_t \textstyle\sum_k f_k(t)\Big)\,|t-s| \;=\; 356\,|t-s|,$$

and the bound is attained exactly — $\omega(\delta) = L\delta$ to every digit for $\delta \le 35$ ms, because at $t = 132.695$ s there is a stretch that long over which $\sum_k f_k \equiv 356$ — so the optimal Hölder exponent of $F$ is exactly $1$. The Cantor function is Hölder of exponent $\log 2/\log 3 \approx 0.6309$ and of no better; it fails to be Lipschitz at every point of the Cantor set. The two objects are therefore in different regularity classes, and the gap is measurable.

the honest version

The Cantor picture was a good guess about the shape and it is wrong about the analysis. What the guess got right is that $F$ is a monotone, continuous, piecewise-affine function that is constant on the silences — the silhouette is a staircase. What it got wrong is everything measured: the flat set has measure 7.5% of the interval rather than 100%, there are 66 plateaus rather than a Cantor set of them, and $F$ is absolutely continuous with $F' = \sum_k f_k \in L^\infty$ rather than singular. Under the pedal it gets further away, not closer: the sounding $F$ has 5 plateaus totalling 2.06 s, so it is strictly increasing on 99.1% of the take.

3The channel you are not using is the one carrying the most

The FP-30X sends two velocity bytes per note: one on the note-on, one on the note-off. Only the first appears in the model above, because only the first scales anything. On this take the second one carries more information than the first.

why this is the interesting result

780 of 804 releases (97%) happened with the damper pedal already down — the string was not going to be stopped, so the speed at which the key came up had no acoustic consequence whatsoever. And yet across those same notes the release byte varies with +0.54 bits more entropy than the strike byte, and its variation is essentially independent of the strike, of the pitch, and (below a second) of the duration. The instrument is measuring a gesture at higher resolution than the one you are consciously shaping, and then discarding it.

Two readings, and this take cannot separate them. Either the release is a real expressive channel you already articulate unconsciously — in which case a synthesis path that honours it has something to work with — or it is uncontrolled noise from a hand leaving a key that no longer matters, in which case its high entropy is precisely because you are not attending to it. The discriminating experiment is a take played with the pedal up, and it has not been done.

4Rhythm and geography

Inter-onset intervals: $n = 797$, mean 277 ms, median 180 ms, coefficient of variation $1.068$. A CV of exactly 1 is the memoryless case, so at the level of the one-dimensional marginal the onsets are indistinguishable from a Poisson process. The Fano curve in §2 says where that stops being true: the index of dispersion is 0.93 at a 100 ms window and 6.08 at 5 s. Below a quarter of a second you place notes as if at random; above a second you clump them, which is what a phrase is.

Note durations are quantised to the same 5 ms lattice as everything else (1 of 804 exceptions) and bottom out at exactly 50 ms — you have no note shorter than one tenth of a second, and the median is 385 ms against a longest of 12.58 s.

5Can these timestamps be trusted?

To 5 ms, yes. Below 5 ms there is nothing here, and no amount of care in the capture layer will produce any, because the floor is upstream of the capture.

The native front end takes the MIDITimeStamp CoreMIDI applies to each packet near the driver, which removed our own 2.08 ms poll-loop quantisation. What it revealed underneath is a harder floor. Of 2185 packets, 2184 (99.95%) lie on a single 5.000 ms lattice; the gaps between consecutive packets take 20 distinct values in the first 100 ms and every one of them is a multiple of 5 ms; 78 of the other 80 bins are empty. Exactly 1 packet in the take is off the lattice, by 1 ms.

against the earlier benchmark, honestly

The 0.0000 ms jitter figure recorded earlier was measured on a synthetic virtual source with no radio in the path. It measured the capture tool and it was right about the capture tool; it said nothing about the link, and it should not be quoted as if it had. This take is the first measurement of the actual Bluetooth path, and the answer is a hard 5.000 ms grid.

The 5.000 ms minimum inter-onset noted on an earlier sample is therefore not a coincidence and not a rounding artifact — it is the grid spacing, and it is the shortest gap the link can express. Two layers are stacked here and the data separates them. BLE-MIDI carries a 13-bit millisecond timestamp, which is why every value is an integer number of milliseconds; the further factor of 5 is the source's own emission cadence, i.e. either the FP-30X scanning its key matrix at 200 Hz or its BLE transmitter batching into 5 ms slots. This capture cannot distinguish those two, and a USB-MIDI take would settle it in one minute.

Consequences worth stating. (a) The link serialises: 2185 of 2185 packets have a distinct timestamp, so a chord arrives as separate events 5 ms apart and true simultaneity is destroyed at the transport — this is what the $V_{\ell^1}/V_{\ell^\infty}$ ratio in §1 is measuring. The exception is the 53 packets that carry two or three messages in one MIDIPacket; those events really were simultaneous, and they are the only simultaneity the link admits. (b) The message rate has a ceiling of 200/s plus bundles. The peak observed here is 160/s in a 100 ms window and 120/s on the control take, so the ~226 msg/s figure from the old poll-loop captures does not reproduce and was almost certainly the poll loop bunching arrivals it had sat on. (c) Nothing was lost: 0 packets dropped, 0 truncated, 0 unstamped, clean trailer.

6What the instrument does not send

Full message census for this take: note_on × 804, note_off × 804, control_change × 632. Three types, nothing else. No channel pressure (0xD0), no polyphonic key pressure (0xA0), no pitch bend, no system exclusive, no active sensing. The action is a discrete-event device: one sample when the hammer is launched, one when the key returns, and nothing at all in between, no matter what the finger does to a key that is already down.

The control take 2026-08-17-wiggle.fp30 (90 s, 125 strikes) was played specifically to try to break that: hold a key and press harder. It produced no additional messages. That is the second independent confirmation, after the five older takes, and this one came through the hardware-timestamped path. It also reproduces the 5 ms lattice — 99.79% of its 482 packets — which is what makes the lattice a property of the link rather than of one recording.

So the whole expressive surface the FP-30X exposes is: which key, when it went down, how fast, when it came up, how fast, and the damper position as a continuous controller (632 CC64 messages, 416 of them strictly between 0 and 127, pedal down for 214 s = 94% of the take across 101 spans). Two of those six are underused: the release byte, per §3, and the intermediate pedal positions, which the threshold-at-64 model in Performance.with_sustain currently throws away wholesale.
